location: Amazon Interview.docx › Tell me about yourself (¶3-5)
heading: Tell me about yourself
text:
I grew up across India and China before moving to the US for college, where I studied Materials Engineering at University of Illinois - I was drawn to understanding how things are built and perform under stress.
After graduation, I spent four years at Otis Elevator Company progressing through three roles in project management. I managed a $47 million portfolio across 50+ construction projects, coordinating installations and stakeholder communication across contractors, architects, and building owners. The highlight of my time at Otis was winning the PM Excellence Award in 2024. But I realized I wanted to transition from construction into tech operations at scale, which is why I'm at Haas pursuing my MBA.
Outside of work, I'm passionate about exploring different cultures through food and travel, and staying active through hiking. I am also an amateur golfer.

location: Amazon Interview.docx › Why Amazon? (¶7-9)
heading: Why Amazon?
text:
I would like to work for Amazon because it’s managed to build the most sophisticated delivery and logistics network in the world. Moreover, it’s also managed to defend that advantage for decades against competitors like Walmart, Target, and now Tiktok Shop. What really sets Amazon apart besides the technology is its operational excellence at a massive scale.
At Otis, I managed a $47M portfolio across 50+ construction projects where I learned that great operations come down to always putting your customer first and delivering on your commitments. When delays cascaded, it directly impacted families moving into buildings or businesses opening on schedule. That experience taught me the same thing I see at Amazon: keep the customer at the center and deliver on your promises.
Whether it’s promising same-day delivery or the use of robotics in fulfillment centers, Amazon continually raises the bar for reliability and speed. I’d love to be part of the team that maintains that operational edge and helps drive the next generation of improvements.

location: Amazon Interview.docx › Why Pathways? (¶11-13)
heading: Why Pathways?
text:
I am drawn to the Pathways program because I don't want to observe operational excellence from a distance - I want to be an active part of it. At Otis, I was most effective on-site with superintendents and mechanics solving real-time problems, not in an office. Similarly, I want to be on the floor of a fulfillment center, speaking with associates, and finding creative ways to improve delivery processes.
Pathways also feels like the natural next step for me as someone who's already worked in operations and managed complex projects. I know how to lead through influence and how to adapt my communication style depending on who I'm speaking to — whether it's a mechanic, a site superintendent, or a senior VP. I've learned that great leadership means meeting people where they are and motivating them to deliver results.
I learn by doing, and the chance to contribute to the world's most efficient delivery operation while learning from leaders who built this system is why I'm excited about this role.

heading: Tell me about a time you had to overcome challenges when working with a team (cross-fun...

location: Amazon Interview.docx › Tell me about a time you used multiple resources to overcome a challenge/had to work un... (¶25-28)
heading: Tell me about a time you used multiple resources to overcome a challenge/had to work un...
text:
Last year, supply chain disruptions increased our material lead times from 10 to 16 weeks, putting multiple projects at risk of significant delays. I had to inform customers of this bad news, and understandably, they were not happy.
I needed to keep projects on schedule despite the delays and maintain customer satisfaction. This was important to me because I had committed to these timelines, and I knew delays would damage both customer relationships and our reputation for reliable delivery.
I took a two-pronged approach leveraging different resources. First, I worked with our factory to implement partial shipments - getting materials shipped as they became available rather than waiting for complete orders. This allowed our mechanics to start assembly immediately with available parts and install missing components later. Second, I coordinated with our field mechanics to put in significant overtime to make up for any remaining schedule gaps and ensure we hit our deadlines.
By strategically using both factory flexibility and mechanic capacity, I kept all projects on track and maintained customer satisfaction despite the supply chain crisis. Customers appreciated the proactive problem-solving, and we didn't lose any projects due to delays.

location: Amazon Interview.docx › Tell me about a time you had disagreement with a colleague/worked with a teammate who w... (¶40-47)
heading: Tell me about a time you had disagreement with a colleague/worked with a teammate who w...
text:
One of our major recurring customers ran out of funds on a project and refused to pay us $125,000 that was owed. He leveraged his status as a key client to avoid payment, creating tension between our company’s financial priorities and the need to maintain a long-term relationship.
Created conflict between Sales and Finance. Sales believed we should write-off the amount to preserve relationship while finance wanted to collect every last penny
I needed to find a solution that secured as much of the payment as possible while preserving the relationship with this key client for future business.
First, I analyzed our internal system to assess the project's financial health. I discovered that even without the additional payment, we would remain net positive overall.
Using this information, I negotiated with the client and proposed a compromise:
We would write off half of the unpaid amount on this project as a one time courtesy discount.
The remaining balance would be deferred into a future project to ensure continued business.
This win-win solution prevented a potential financial loss and protected our long-term relationship with the client. The customer appreciated the flexibility, and we continued doing business together, ensuring future revenue.

location: Amazon Interview.docx › Tell me about a time you dug into data/used data to inform/change your decision? (¶49-54)
heading: Tell me about a time you dug into data/used data to inform/change your decision?
text:
- San Jose office was facing a serious cash flow issue because of $7 million in invoices that were unpaid & significantly overdue, which represented 33% of total AR
- My manager asked me to come up with recommendations on how to address the issue.
- I started off by segmenting the data based on the different lines of business at Otis to see where the issue was concentrated. I found out that the new construction line of business accounted for 55% of the overdue AR, which was disproportionately high.
- After looking at the quantitative data, I decided to interview other internal stakeholders to try and get to the root cause. During interviews, I found out the major issues were that PM’s were not getting notified when invoices were sent out, we had regional collectors who were spread too thin, and liens were not being filed strategically.
- Based on data, I presented three solutions to leadership, which were thankfully all approved and we saw a 15% drop in AR.
- I am most proud that I didn’t stop at just the numbers. Data showed me what was wrong & the interviews revealed why. Both qualitative and quantitative data were essential to solving this problem.

location: Amazon Interview.docx › Tell me about ways that you personally have tried to mature the engineering efforts on... (¶56-66)
heading: Tell me about ways that you personally have tried to mature the engineering efforts on...
text:
• I noticed our customers repeatedly asked the same technical questions about elevator codes and design requirements.
• Project managers—and sometimes engineers—were spending unnecessary time rewriting the same explanations.
• This created inconsistent answers for our customers, slower response times, and a lot of duplicated effort across the team.
• To solve this, I created a centralized reference folder that included:

• It also improved customer satisfaction by shortening response times and reducing escalations.
• Overall, it was a significant change that made our engineering and project delivery process more consistent, and efficient.

location: Amazon Interview.docx › Tell me a time you failed/ received negative feedback. (¶68-78)
heading: Tell me a time you failed/ received negative feedback.
text:
When at Otis, I received critical feedback after a design decision I made did not follow standard operating procedures.
I was managing a project for a demanding client who requested premium customizations, including heavy wood wall panels and Italian marble flooring inside the elevator cab.
• My responsibility was to ensure the elevator met all design specifications, including strict weight limits, before releasing it into fabrication.
• Under schedule pressure, I made a judgment call without completing the full SOP verification.
• I performed rapid mental calculations and approved the design for fabrication without formally verifying the final cab weight, which was a required step in our SOP.
• This backfired as the elevator cab was over the maximum weight limit, which meant that it would fail final state inspections.
- When the issue was later identified, I immediately acknowledged the mistake rather than deflecting blame.
• I worked with engineering and the client to redesign the cab, ultimately replacing the marble flooring with thin-set tiles to bring the cab back within weight limits.
• The redesign caused project delays and resulted in financial losses for Otis, which was the basis of the feedback I received.
• I took full ownership of the outcome and focused on preventing a repeat.
• I created a pre-fabrication checklist that highlighted the most common pitfalls, I and shared it with other project managers.

location: Tanium Interview Prep.docx › What did you do at Otis? (¶14-18)
heading: What did you do at Otis?
text:
At Otis, I was a project manager managing a $47M portfolio of 50+ new construction elevator projects simultaneously. My role had three main focus areas:
First, stakeholder coordination: I had to align multiple internal and external parties - contractors, architects, city officials, building owners - who all had different priorities and timelines. I had no direct authority over most of them, so I had to rely on leadership without formal power and bridge organizational silos to keep everyone aligned.
Second, risk management at scale: With 50+ projects running concurrently, issues emerged constantly. I had to monitor for early warning signs, flag problems before they escalated, and coordinate rapid responses to prevent them from cascading into larger project failures. This meant developing a sense of pattern recognition for common failure and building relationships so stakeholders would escalate issues early rather than trying to solve them independently.
Third, technical problem-solving: I was responsible for handling any technical challenges - design modifications, code compliance issues, construction conflicts - which meant quickly understanding complex problems, coming up with a game plan, and then getting team buy off in order to execute this game plan.
Finally, beyond the three main focus areas, I had full P&L responsibility for the portfolio and was accountable for hitting financial metrics across all projects.

location: Tanium Interview Prep.docx › Why Cybersecurity & Tanium? (¶20-22)
heading: Why Cybersecurity & Tanium?
text:
My interest in cybersecurity actually started off with a canceled flight. Last year in July, I was supposed to fly Delta, but because of the CrowdStrike outage my flight was cancelled. I was annoyed in the moment, but also genuinely curious on how a single update could take down systems all around the world? That question led me down a rabbit hole because I wanted to understand the technical and operational failures that led to this catastrophe. And like anytime I’m genuinely curious about something, I ended up on Reddit reading threads from people way smarter — and way angrier — than I was.
That curiosity pushed me deeper into endpoint security. I started comparing different companies in the space and Tanium kept appearing in those comparisons. I’d driven past your Emeryville office countless times and seen the huge Tanium logo on the building, but this was the first time I truly understood the significance of what you were building.
After speaking with [former Tanium intern] who interned here last year and learning more about Tanium’s mission, it felt like everything aligned — the type of problems you solve, the scale you operate at, and the way the company thinks about risk. That’s why Tanium stood out to me, and why I’m excited about the opportunity today.

location: Tanium Interview Prep.docx › What does Tanium do? (¶24-26)
heading: What does Tanium do?
text:
Tanium is an endpoint management and security platform that gives IT departments real-time visibility and control over all endpoints - laptops, servers, smartphones, and any other devices connected to the company's network.
What sets Tanium apart from competitors are two key innovations: First is their ability to query all endpoints in under 15 seconds, thanks to the linear chain architecture, which dramatically reduces server load. (2) Its unified platform of modules that cover the full lifecycle: security, operations, patching, compliance, incident response, asset discovery, automation, and more. Tools like Tanium Guardian provide proactive vulnerability monitoring, while Tanium Automate lets teams execute playbooks and workflows that simplify everything from patching to onboarding new devices.
Instead of stitching together multiple solutions for asset management, patching, EDR, compliance, and configuration, Tanium consolidates them into one platform. That’s why many enterprises think of Tanium as the backbone of their IT and security operations — real-time, accurate, and massively scalable.

heading: Tell me about how you have stayed current on industry developments over the course of y...
text:
As I’ve shifted toward product management in tech, I’ve made a deliberate effort to stay current on industry developments. I do that in a few ways. First, I try to stay plugged into the ecosystem through conferences, PM workshops, and tech-focused events at Haas. These helps me build relationships with people who are actually working through these problems.
I also like to understand the ‘why’ behind things. The CrowdStrike outage last summer is a good example — the scale of the failure made me dig deeper into security and patching and it is what led me to learn more about Tanium’s philosophy around real-time visibility and more controlled rollouts.

Recently, I used Claude for Vibe Coding to create a minimum viable product (MVP) for a personal problem: I have way too many credit cards, and I kept forgetting which one gave the best rewards in different scenarios. So I built a web app that categorizes my cards and tells me which one to use based on the scenario I am in. This is what helped me get hands-on with developments in AI and no-code tooling.
Finally, conversations play a big role. Talking with people in the space — including a recent conversation with [former Tanium intern] at Tanium — helps me understand how practitioners see emerging trends and where the real challenges are.

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › How does Tiktok monetize? (¶12-20)
heading: How does Tiktok monetize?
text:
- Ads: In-feed (every 2 to 3 videos) & top view ads (as soon as you open the app).
- Tiktok shop: Charges seller commission on every transaction & sellers have to pay to advertise their products. HIGHEST growth over the past two years.
- Brand partnerships – Hashtag challenges, Brand takeover days, Brand Awareness campaign.
- Gifts to Creators- When people give roses or galaxies to creators to show appreciation, tiktok gets a cut.
Sample Answer:
TikTok has four main revenue streams, with advertising being the largest.
First, advertising - primarily through in-feed ads that appear every 2-3 videos in the For You Page, and TopView ads that take over the screen when users first open the app. This is their core revenue driver.
Second, TikTok Shop, which has seen the highest growth over the past two years. They monetize this in two ways: taking a commission on every transaction, typically 2-8% depending on category, and charging sellers to advertise their products on the platform. This creates a dual revenue stream where TikTok profits both from the sale itself and from the ads driving traffic to those products.
Third, brand partnerships - these are premium, high-value deals like branded hashtag challenges where brands pay $150K-500K+, brand takeover days for exclusive daily placement, and large-scale brand awareness campaigns. These command premium pricing compared to standard advertising.

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › How does Tiktok monetize? (¶20-22)
heading: How does Tiktok monetize?
text:
Third, brand partnerships - these are premium, high-value deals like branded hashtag challenges where brands pay $150K-500K+, brand takeover days for exclusive daily placement, and large-scale brand awareness campaigns. These command premium pricing compared to standard advertising.
And fourth, virtual gifts - when users send gifts like roses or galaxies to creators during LIVE streams to show appreciation, TikTok takes a cut of those transactions before paying out creators.
The key insight is that TikTok Shop's growth shows they're successfully diversifying beyond pure advertising into commerce, which improves their revenue resilience and deepens user engagement on the platform

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › Who are Tiktok’s competitors and what are their strengths? (¶24-30)
heading: Who are Tiktok’s competitors and what are their strengths?
text:
Sample Answer:
Meta's biggest strength is cross-platform targeting which means it can track users across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger,
from a monetization perspective, they can give advertisers incredibly rich data and the ability to reach users across multiple touchpoints.
They also have deep user data from two decades of social networking, which enables sophisticated targeting that TikTok is still building.
YouTube's strength is their unmatched scale - they have over 2 billion monthly users globally and offer both long-form and short-form content with Shorts, which means they can monetize both forms of video content.
They also benefit from Google's ad tech infrastructure, which is the most sophisticated in the industry with advanced analytics, attribution, and measurement tools that advertisers trust.
- Amazon competes directly with TikTok Shop, and their strength is unbeatable logistics and delivery speed. Their fulfillment infrastructure is so advanced that you can order something at 1 AM and have it delivered by 8 AM the same morning. TikTok Shop simply can't match that level of operational excellence and customer trust in delivery reliability. Amazon also has decades of customer reviews, return policies, and Prime loyalty that TikTok is years away from replicating.

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › What are Tiktok’s strengths? (¶32-46)
heading: What are Tiktok’s strengths?
text:
Algorithm Superiority:
- Best in class recommendations
- Keeps users engaged longer
- Markes ads feel native to the app. Ads feel like just another reel
- Introducting long format videos to compete with the likes of YT. Uploaded reels can now be up to 60 mins.
Users:
- Gen Z dominant.
- Highly engaged audience that drives a high engagement rate with plenty of comments, likes and sharing of reels.
Tiktok Shop Integration:
- Seamless purchasing experience
- Live Shopping and Flash Sales create urgency
- Lower barrier for impulse buys.
TikTok has three core competitive advantages that set them apart.
First, algorithm superiority - they have best-in-class content recommendations that keep users engaged significantly longer than competitors. What's particularly powerful is that their algorithm makes ads feel native to the platform - ads blend seamlessly into the feed and feel like just another piece of content rather than an interruption. This is crucial for advertisers because users don't skip or tune out.
Second, their user base and engagement - TikTok is Gen Z dominant, and this demographic is incredibly active on the platform spending around 95 mins on the app every day, which is far higher than competitors. They don't just passively watch; they drive high engagement rates through comments, likes, and sharing content. This creates a viral flywheel that advertisers can tap into, where content spreads organically much faster than on other platforms.

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › What are Tiktok’s strengths? (¶47-48)
heading: What are Tiktok’s strengths?
text:
Third, TikTok Shop integration - they've built a seamless in-app purchasing experience that removes friction from discovery to purchase. Features like live shopping and flash sales create urgency and FOMO, and the impulse-buy barrier is incredibly low since users never have to leave the app. You can go from watching a video to completing a purchase in seconds, which drives significantly higher conversion rates than directing users to external websites.
Together, these strengths create an ecosystem where content, commerce, and community reinforce each other - users are engaged, ads feel authentic, and purchases happen seamlessly.

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › What are the different types of ads and what metrics would you use? (¶50-52)
heading: What are the different types of ads and what metrics would you use?
text:
Top of funnel - Awareness: The goal is pure reach - get the brand in front of as many relevant people as possible. I'd use TopView ads and Brand Takeovers for maximum visibility, tracking metrics like Impressions, Reach, Frequency, and Brand Awareness Lift. At this stage, we're NOT focused on sales - we're building recognition.
Middle of funnel - Consideration: Once people know the brand, we shift to building interest. Now we're retargeting people who engaged with our awareness content using In-Feed Ads with clear CTAs and product demos. The metrics that matter are Click-Through Rate, Time on Site, Email signups, and Add-to-Cart actions. We're getting people to seriously consider the purchase and comparing favorably to competitors.
Bottom of funnel - Conversion: This is where we focus on financial performance - driving actual sales from people who've shown purchase intent. We'd retarget cart abandoners and site visitors with conversion-optimized ads or flash sales which drive FOMO and get people to purchase products. focusing on ROAS, CPA, Conversion Rate, and Revenue.

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › Tell me about a time you had to overcome challenges when working with a team (cross-fun... (¶55-62)
heading: Tell me about a time you had to overcome challenges when working with a team (cross-fun...
text:
- On my largest project to date, Graton Casino Expansion, a $2.9M project, I was coordinating between our internal teams and external stakeholders including architects, general contractors, and global supply vendors.
- The challenge here was that everyone had competing priorities. The customer wanted premium customizations, vendors were pushing back on the timeline stating that this was not feasible and my internal team was worried about scope creep.
- My task was to align all of these different parties and deliver the project without any overruns or delays.
- Established weekly coordination meetings
- Purpose was to understand each team’s constrains and then coming up with compromises like identifying which customizations we could adopt without impacting deadlines greatly
- Presented all possible options to the client with cost and time implications.
- The result was that we delivered the $2.9M project with over $400k in customizations on schedule.
- The structured communication prevented small misalignments from becoming major conflicts, and the client was satisfied with both the process and outcome.

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › Tell me about a time you used multiple resources to overcome a challenge/had to work un... (¶64-67)
heading: Tell me about a time you used multiple resources to overcome a challenge/had to work un...
text:
Last year, supply chain disruptions increased our material lead times from 12 to 16 weeks, putting multiple projects at risk of significant delays. I had to inform customers of this bad news, and understandably, they were not happy.
I needed to keep projects on schedule despite the delays and maintain customer satisfaction. This was important to me because I had committed to these timelines, and I knew delays would damage both customer relationships and our reputation for reliable delivery.
I took a two-pronged approach leveraging different resources. First, I worked with our factory to implement partial shipments - getting materials shipped as they became available rather than waiting for complete orders. This allowed our mechanics to start assembly immediately with available parts and install missing components later. Second, I coordinated with our field mechanics to put in significant overtime to make up for any remaining schedule gaps and ensure we hit our deadlines.
By strategically using both factory flexibility and mechanic capacity, I kept all projects on track and maintained customer satisfaction despite the supply chain crisis. Customers appreciated the proactive problem-solving, and we didn't lose any projects due to delays.

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › Tell me about a time you had disagreement with a colleague/worked with a teammate who w... (¶79-86)
heading: Tell me about a time you had disagreement with a colleague/worked with a teammate who w...
text:
One of our major recurring customers ran out of funds on a project and refused to pay us $125,000 that was owed. He leveraged his status as a key client to avoid payment, creating tension between our company’s financial priorities and the need to maintain a long-term relationship.
Created conflict between Sales and Finance. Sales believed we should write-off the amount to preserve relationship while finance wanted to collect every last penny
I needed to find a solution that secured as much of the payment as possible while preserving the relationship with this key client for future business.
First, I analyzed our internal system to assess the project's financial health. I discovered that even without the additional payment, we would remain net positive overall.
Using this information, I negotiated with the client and proposed a compromise:
We would write off half of the unpaid amount on this project as a one time courtesy discount.
The remaining balance would be deferred into a future project to ensure continued business.
This win-win solution prevented a potential financial loss and protected our long-term relationship with the client. The customer appreciated the flexibility, and we continued doing business together, ensuring future revenue.

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › Tell me about a time you dug into data/used data to inform/change your decision? (¶88-92)
heading: Tell me about a time you dug into data/used data to inform/change your decision?
text:
- San Jose office was facing a serious cash flow issue because of $7 million in invoices that were 90 days overdue, which represented 34% of total AR
- I started by segmenting the data to see where the issue was concentrated. I found out that my line of business accounted for 55% of the overdue AR, which was disproportionately high.
- After looking at the quantitative data, I decided to interview other internal stakeholders to find out why and get to the root cause. During interviews, I found out PM’s were not getting notified when invoices were sent out, we had regional collectors who were spread too thin, and liens were not being filed strategically.
- Based on data, I presented three solutions to leadership, which were thankfully all approved and we saw a 15% drop in AR.
- I am most proud that I didn’t stop at just the numbers. Data showed me what was wrong & the interviews revealed why. Both qualitative and quantitative data were essential to solving this problem.

location: Tiktok Interview Prep.docx › Why do you want to work for Tiktok and why MSO? (¶95-97)
heading: Why do you want to work for Tiktok and why MSO?
text:
I’m drawn to TikTok because it’s a trendsetter in a highly competitive industry and revolutionized how brands approach marketing — from the polished ads we used to see on TV to a more raw, unpolished, and authentic experience that really connects with Gen Z audiences who value connection over perfection. I think that shift in how brands communicate is incredibly powerful.
I want to work in MSO because I love working on monetization, revenue and really increasing bottom line revenue for my products. This interest in monetization and revenue building stems from Otis and its business model. Almost every project that I worked on at Otis was sold at cost, 0% margin, and it was up to me to turn this ship around and hit my profit goals of 5-10%. I became obsesses with finding every lever to drive revenue, whether it was negotiationg with supliers to get better pricing on materials, working with mechanics to figure out a more effeicient installation process or upselling products and service to our customers. I loved using insights and turning operational efficiency into financial results.
I’m especially excited about the Monetization Strategy & Ops team because it sits right at the intersection of creativity, data, and business impact. The team’s focus on understanding revenue trends, optimizing ad effectiveness, and launching new monetization models aligns perfectly with my background, which is combining execution skills from project management with an analytical, data-driven mindset
